title: Vinesh Phogat Fought the Courts, the Federation, and the Mat. She Lost on the Mat.
excerpt: The three-time Olympian won a Supreme Court battle to compete in the Asian Games wrestling trials. A day later, a semifinal loss to Meenakshi Goyat ended her comeback before it truly began.
body:
Vinesh Phogat's comeback lasted twenty-three hours. That is how long it took between the Supreme Court clearing her to wrestle and Meenakshi Goyat pinning her hopes to the canvas at the Indira Gandhi Stadium in New Delhi.

The three-time Olympian lost 4-6 in the semifinal of the women's 53kg category at the Asian Games 2026 selection trials on Saturday. She will not be going to Aichi-Nagoya.

## The Legal Battle That Preceded the Sporting One

Vinesh had not competed since the Paris Olympics, where the world watched her disqualification on the morning of a gold medal bout become one of the most wrenching moments in Indian sporting history. She took a maternity break, gave birth in July 2025, and informed the Wrestling Federation of India that she would return to competition in January 2026.

The WFI had other plans. A circular mandated that only medal winners from the 2025 National Championship and the 2026 Federation Cup could enter the selection trials. Vinesh, who had been on maternity leave during both events, was shut out.

She took the fight to the Delhi High Court, which ruled in her favour on May 22. The judgment was unambiguous: motherhood cannot be treated as a disability or a reason to deny professional opportunities. The court directed the WFI to let her compete and ordered independent observers from the Sports Authority of India and the Indian Olympic Association to monitor the trials.

The WFI challenged the ruling in the Supreme Court. On May 29, a bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe heard arguments and refused to stay the High Court order.

"If it were anybody else, it would have been on a different footing," the bench observed. "She has made the country proud."

The court added a message for Vinesh: "You have been an excellent athlete. But country first."

## Two Wins, Then a Wall

Vinesh weighed in at 53.9 kg on Saturday morning. By afternoon, she had dispatched Jyoti of Haryana 7-1 in her opening bout, using a combination of standing wrestling and devastating takedowns that suggested the time away had not dulled her instincts.

Her second bout against Nishu was more gruelling. Nishu opened a massive 5-0 lead and nearly pinned Vinesh with a spectacular four-point throw in the first period. But the veteran survived, clawed back, and won — a performance that married experience with sheer will.

The semifinal against Meenakshi Goyat, an Asian Championships silver medallist, was the wall she could not scale. The bout was intensely physical and emotionally charged, interrupted by technical failures of the display screens and several challenges from both corners. The long breaks gave Vinesh time to recover between exchanges, but they could not compensate for the toll that months away from competitive wrestling had taken on her endurance.

Meenakshi won 6-4. It was over.

Vinesh and her husband, fellow wrestler Somvir Rathee, said afterward that they felt "cheated" by the refereeing. The accusation added one more layer of controversy to a day already soaked in it.

## Antim Takes the Berth — Amid More Controversy

Meenakshi's own campaign ended in the final, where two-time U20 world champion Antim Panghal edged her 3-2 in another tightly contested bout. Meenakshi's camp protested the officiating in the final as well, with her coach publicly accusing the referee of bias. She has since filed a formal complaint with the WFI.

WFI President Sanjay Singh confirmed receipt of the complaint but said the result would stand. Antim will represent India at the Asian Games.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the millions of Indians worldwide who had followed Vinesh's legal battle — from the High Court's landmark ruling on motherhood and sport to the Supreme Court's pointed observation about national pride — Saturday's outcome was a gut punch delivered not by institutions but by the sport itself.

The principle was established: a female athlete cannot be excluded from competition for choosing to become a mother. That precedent stands regardless of what happened on the mat. But the comeback narrative that so many NRIs had invested in — the story of an Olympic champion returning from motherhood to reclaim her place at the top — ended at the semifinal stage of a domestic trial.

Vinesh is thirty-two years old. She is a sitting MLA from Julana in Haryana. Whether she returns to the mat is a question only she can answer. What she has already done — in courts and on the canvas — will outlast any single result.

The Asian Games are in Aichi-Nagoya later this year. Antim Panghal will be there. Vinesh Phogat will not.
author: Diaspora Desk
